action_criteria.expected_evidence: Three non-contiguous enhancing lesions: dominant 4.8 cm right parieto-occipital mass with thick irregular septated ring enhancement, central necrosis, rim restriction and FLAIR signal extending well beyond enhancement into the splenium, with 6 mm midline shift; a 1.9 cm nodular right frontal lesion; a 1.2 cm ring-enhancing left superior temporal lesion at the gray-white junction
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol with DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to characterize the multifocal enhancing lesions, define mass effect, and establish the dominant biopsy target
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast MRI characterizes the multifocal lesions, defines the mass effect and selects the dominant lesion as the tissue target (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: rCBV 4.1 at the dominant rim and 2.3 in the non-enhancing perilesional FLAIR tissue, which favors an infiltrating glioma over metastatic edema
action_criteria.label: Order MR perfusion imaging (DSC-MRI) to assess perilesional rCBV and guide differential between multicentric glioma and brain metastases
action_criteria.rationale: Raised perilesional rCBV indicates infiltrating tumor; edema around metastases usually has normal rCBV. Tissue decides the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Cho/NAA 6.1 in the enhancing rim and 3.4 in the non-enhancing FLAIR zone, favoring an infiltrating glioma over metastasis
action_criteria.label: Order MR spectroscopy (1H-MRS) with voxels in the enhancing rim and the non-enhancing perilesional FLAIR zone to assess for tumor infiltration beyond visible lesion boundaries
action_criteria.rationale: Choline elevation in non-enhancing perilesional tissue favors infiltrating glioma over the vasogenic edema of a metastasis; tissue decides.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right parieto-occipital focal delta slowing and occasional left mid temporal sharp waves; no electrographic seizure
action_criteria.label: Obtain an EEG to characterize the episode of speech arrest with staring
action_criteria.rationale: A 15-second speech arrest with staring and unawareness in a patient with a left temporal lesion is a focal seizure; the EEG characterizes it and supports the antiseizure treatment (AIOM supportive care).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No extracranial malignancy or lymphadenopathy; an indeterminate 1.3 cm hepatic lesion; no recurrence at the melanoma site
action_criteria.label: Order CT chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast to look for systemic melanoma recurrence or another primary
action_criteria.rationale: Required: a prior melanoma and multiple enhancing lesions make systemic staging part of the work-up before a primary brain tumor is accepted.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, platelets and coagulation (PT 13.1 s, INR 1.0, aPTT 31 s); LDH 312 U/L and S100B 0.18 µg/L raised but non-specific; no contraindication to surgery
action_criteria.label: Order pre-operative laboratory workup: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies and type and screen
action_criteria.rationale: Platelets, coagulation and type and screen must be known before a neurosurgical procedure; potassium matters on hydrochlorothiazide with dexamethasone.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: KPS 70, ECOG 2: independent in self-care, unable to work because of cognitive decline, mild left hemiparesis and quadrantanopia
action_criteria.label: Score the current performance status (Karnofsky and ECOG) at this visit
action_criteria.rationale: The pre-illness KPS 80 is not the current value; KPS below 70 is the unfavourable threshold, and in multicentric glioblastoma it decides whether cytoreduction and chemoradiation are offered (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Integrated diagnosis Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 with IDH1 R132H negative, no IDH1/IDH2 mutation, ATRX retained, MGMT promoter unmethylated, and SOX10, Melan-A and HMB-45 negative
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by stereotactic biopsy of the dominant right parieto-occipital lesion, or cytoreductive resection of it, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, IDH1/IDH2 sequencing (age under 55), ATRX, MGMT promoter methylation and the melanocytic markers SOX10, Melan-A and HMB-45
action_criteria.rationale: In multicentric disease, biopsy of the dominant lesion comes first, and resection is cytoreduction of that lesion only (EANO 2021). Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis, and the melanocytic markers exclude a melanoma metastasis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Potassium loss with dexamethasone and hydrochlorothiazide; gastric protection with aspirin; aspirin timing before surgery; no levetiracetam interaction

action_criteria.rationale: Optional: no interaction changes the diagnostic plan.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture: the 6 mm midline shift and effacement of the right occipital horn carry a herniation risk
Do not diagnose brain metastases and initiate whole-brain radiotherapy or systemic melanoma therapy without tissue confirmation
Do not initiate tumor-directed therapy (temozolomide, immunotherapy) before histomolecular tissue diagnosis is established
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for stereotactic biopsy of the dominant right parieto-occipital lesion, with cytoreductive resection of that lesion as the alternative when the performance status allows; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Start antiseizure treatment with levetiracetam for the documented focal seizure (15 seconds of speech arrest with staring and unawareness); this is treatment of tumour-related epilepsy, not prophylaxis. Avoid enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), which lower dexamethasone and chemotherapy exposure.

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.
Include the melanocytic markers SOX10, Melan-A and HMB-45 in the pathology panel to exclude melanoma metastasis
Stop aspirin 7 days before biopsy or craniotomy, and advise him not to drive after the seizure.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, at age 52 with KPS 70, radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions covering all three lesions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021), noting that the unmethylated MGMT promoter predicts a smaller temozolomide benefit; if the KPS falls below 70, hypofractionated radiotherapy.

metadata.real_seed_note: Seeded from: 'Glioblastoma Masquerading as Metastasis in a Routine Follow-Up of a 79-Year-Old Woman' (PMID 40291335, PMC12024517, CC-BY 4.0). Confirmed multicentric GBM IDH-wildtype WHO grade 4 presenting as multiple ring-enhancing lesions initially attributed to metastatic disease from prior breast DCIS. Demographics, clinical details, melanoma history, lab values, and MRI characteristics were independently authored for NeuroBench; only the core puzzle concept (multicentric GBM mimicking metastases in a patient with prior cancer history) is seeded from the published case.

patient.history_present_illness: This 52-year-old right-handed African-American man, a high school principal with a history of excised cutaneous melanoma, presents to the neurology service for evaluation of progressive headaches and cognitive changes over the past seven weeks. His spouse is the primary historian and prompted this evaluation after the patient minimized his symptoms. Approximately seven weeks ago he began experiencing persistent right-sided headaches, which he described as a pressure sensation rather than pulsatile pain, prominent upon awakening in the morning and exacerbated by leaning forward. Acetaminophen provided partial relief. Over the ensuing four weeks, his spouse began noticing behavioral and cognitive changes that were distinctly out of character: he twice missed administrative meetings he himself had scheduled, repeatedly asked the same questions within a few minutes, left his school office unlocked on three occasions, something he had never done in 18 years as principal, and had difficulty composing a formal letter that would previously have taken him minutes. He was seen by his primary care physician approximately five weeks ago who attributed symptoms to work stress. Ten days prior to the current presentation, his spouse witnessed an episode in which the patient abruptly stopped mid-sentence during dinner, stared blankly with a slightly glassy expression for approximately 15 seconds, then resumed conversation. He appeared unaware of the interruption and denied any subjective experience. There was no convulsive activity, loss of consciousness, or post-event confusion. This episode prompted urgent neurological referral. He denies fever, chills, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, or changes in skin lesions. Of substantial clinical concern is his history of cutaneous melanoma of the right posterior shoulder, resected three years ago with confirmed negative sentinel lymph node. He remains in the recommended five-year surveillance protocol; his last dermatological examination five months ago was unremarkable, and a PET-CT performed eleven months ago revealed no evidence of metastatic disease. His current medications are amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, and low-dose aspirin. He is a former smoker with a 12-pack-year history, quit 15 years ago. He drinks alcohol occasionally. He sleeps with CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea.

neurological_exam.additional: Spouse reports a 7-week history of progressive change: the patient initially complained of persistent right-sided headaches, worse in the morning and on bending forward, partially relieved by acetaminophen. Over the past 4 weeks, she noticed he had become unusually forgetful — missing scheduled meetings at school, leaving his office unlocked, repeating questions he had asked minutes earlier. He had one witnessed episode approximately 10 days ago consisting of sudden cessation of speech, blank staring for 15 seconds, then return to conversation, unaware of the interruption, without post-ictal confusion. No generalized convulsive activity. He downplays cognitive change and attributes it to work stress.
